justifications.functional_suitability: All requirements are fulfilled: Scoring Executor Component evaluates transactions (R-01), Case Management API with Case Service facilitates reviews (R-02), and In-Memory Model Cache Component with Rule & Model Cache enables zero-downtime model and rule hot-reloading (R-03).
justifications.performance_efficiency: The sub-50ms P99 target at 3,000 RPS is addressed using Go on ECS, gRPC over mTLS, local WASM evaluation, Redis Feature Store caching, and decoupling heavy audit writes via Asynchronous Messaging (Amazon SQS).
justifications.compatibility: Standard protocols ensure seamless integration: gRPC/mTLS interfaces with Payment Gateway / Acquirer, OIDC/OAuth 2.0 integrates Identity Provider (IdP), and standard PostgreSQL Wire Protocol and Redis Protocol connect internal data stores.
justifications.usability: Fraud Analysts are supported via Case Management Ingress Router and Case Management API with RBAC. However, the architecture defines only backend APIs without detailing the frontend web application interface used by analysts.
justifications.reliability: High availability is supported via Multi-AZ ElastiCache, SQS DLQs, and Feature Aggregator Component timeout fallbacks. However, an explicit circuit-breaker or fail-open mechanism ensuring payments are unblocked within 1 minute (R-07) is missing.
justifications.security: Security thoroughly addresses PCI-DSS L1: API Handler Component performs PAN tokenization, Audit Sink leverages S3 Object Lock, Auth & RBAC Middleware secures sessions, and ALB enforces TLS 1.3, mTLS, and AWS WAF inspection.
justifications.maintainability: Modular design separates concerns between Fraud Scoring Engine and Case Management API. Zero-downtime hot-swapping in Scoring Executor Component and managed AWS services ensure low operational overhead for a 3-engineer team.
justifications.portability: Targeted specifically to AWS eu-west-1 using containerized services (Go/Node.js on ECS). However, tight integration with AWS-native services (SQS, S3 Object Lock, AWS WAF, ALB) limits portability to other cloud environments.

PERF-01.justification: While Go, in-memory channels, and local WASM execution minimize processing overhead, the Fraud Scoring Engine writes directly to PostgreSQL on the synchronous path, creating a substantial latency bottleneck that jeopardizes the 50 ms P99 SLA at 3,000 TPS.
sensitivity_points: Direct synchronous database writes during transaction scoring under peak throughput
Redis network round-trip time for sliding-window velocity counters
tradeoffs: Immediate relational persistence vs. sub-50 ms decision latency under peak load

PERF-02.justification: Complete path and workload separation is enforced at the ALB. Analyst traffic is routed to a dedicated Case Management API and isolated RDS read replica, ensuring heavy analyst queries never contend with scoring engine resources.
sensitivity_points: Isolation of analyst query execution on the RDS Read Replica
tradeoffs: Replication lag on read replicas vs. eliminating contention on the primary database

AVAIL-01.justification: The architecture lacks a stand-in or fallback decision mechanism if the scoring engine crashes. While Redis features have local fallbacks, total container failure leaves no automated bypass or rule-based stand-in at the ingress layer.
sensitivity_points: Absence of edge or load-balancer fallback rules when scoring targets are unhealthy
tradeoffs: Strict screening enforcement vs. rapid fail-open or stand-in payment authorization

AVAIL-02.justification: Audit logging is fully decoupled from the critical path using an asynchronous Audit Dispatcher pushing to Amazon SQS. SQS buffers audit events, and a Dead-Letter Queue handles retries if downstream audit sinks degrade.
sensitivity_points: SQS queue capacity and retention buffer during extended audit sink outages
tradeoffs: Eventual consistency of audit trails vs. zero latency impact on authorization decisions

MOD-01.justification: The scoring engine leverages local WASM binaries cached in memory and dynamic rule stores in Redis. The In-Memory Model Cache atomically hot-swaps cryptographically verified models without container restarts, enabling immediate rollbacks.
sensitivity_points: Atomic pointer swapping for WASM binaries in the in-memory cache
tradeoffs: In-memory model execution limits model complexity vs. providing sub-millisecond execution and instant swaps

MOD-02.justification: Rules are fetched dynamically from the Redis Rule & Model Cache and evaluated in the Scoring Executor. Decisions explicitly capture applied rule IDs, and updates take effect dynamically across scoring instances without redeployment.
sensitivity_points: Polling interval or pub/sub latency for Redis rule cache synchronization
tradeoffs: Dynamic rule parsing overhead vs. zero-downtime hot reloading

SEC-01.justification: The API Handler sanitizes and tokenizes PANs at ingress, preventing plain-text card storage in case repositories. However, the architecture specifies no automated anomaly detection, SIEM integration, or behavioral alerting to detect compromised accounts within 15 minutes.
sensitivity_points: Completeness of PAN tokenization at ingress before data reaches case storage
tradeoffs: Tokenization security vs. analyst investigation capability without seeing raw PANs

SEC-02.justification: A 7-year retention strategy is explicitly addressed via pg_partman automated partitioning and archival to S3 Glacier Vault and S3 Object Lock. Immutable audit logs store decision inputs, model versions, and HMAC signatures, meeting the retrieval timeline.
sensitivity_points: S3 Object Lock retention policy and Glacier retrieval turnaround time
tradeoffs: Cold storage retrieval latency vs. low-cost compliance over a 7-year lifecycle
